title: The Sinking City

aoi.name: California Aqueduct corridor, Huron – Kettleman City, San Joaquin Valley, California
aoi.source: ../sars/07_NISAR_StoryMaps/Land_Subsidence/Land_Subsidence_narrative.md (case study 'Central Valley Groundwater Subsidence'; bowl extent read from the graticule of resources/Jj5OZk8y7-J7ZxXUZjRxg.png, UAVSAR line 14511, 36°00'–36°12' N, 119°58'–120°08' W); ../sars/09_UAVSAR_Postcards/postcards.csv (row 'Huron and Kettleman City', July 2013 – March 2015); docs/ARCHITECTURE.md §9

briefing.question: Where has the ground changed?
briefing.summary: Farms along the California Aqueduct pump groundwater, and the land above can sink. Follow ten months of radar passes and mark the ground that keeps going down.
body: This is the San Joaquin Valley between Huron and Kettleman City. The aqueduct carries water south right through it.
Every step is a real NISAR pass: track 042, descending, frame 070. The ground motion you see is SIMULATED for this case. Only the dates and the orbit geometry are real.
Some changes are just weather in the radar signal. They show up once and are gone on the next pass. Look for ground that keeps sinking, step after step.
Hatched areas had low radar coherence on that pass, so there is nothing reliable to read there.
Two passes are missing from the record. They are marked "No acquisition", and nothing is filled in for them.
Pick two dates at least 24 days apart, outline your region and validate it. The score compares your region with an authored answer mask. It is a mission score, not a scientific measurement.
briefing.location: California Aqueduct corridor, Huron – Kettleman City, San Joaquin Valley, California · 36.14° N, 120.09° W
briefing.dates: 31 Dec 2025 – 15 Oct 2026 · 9 passes, every third 12-day cycle · 2 with no acquisition
briefing.source: Dates, track and frame: NISAR catalogue (NASA CMR, ASF DAAC). Displacement and coherence: SIMULATED by BlindRev data-forge. Context imagery: NASA GIBS (HLS S30 Sentinel-2 true colour — contains modified Copernicus Sentinel-2 data; MODIS Terra; NISAR GCOV; Blue Marble).

facts.text: In 2014, the second year of extreme drought, pumping opened a subsidence bowl across the California Aqueduct. The closest parts of the canal sank more than 12 inches.
Airborne radar (UAVSAR) watched the same bowl from June 2013 to November 2017. Parts of it sank more than 40 inches.
facts.source: ../sars/07_NISAR_StoryMaps/Land_Subsidence/Land_Subsidence_narrative.md (l.48; Miller et al. 2020, Remote Sensing of Environment 251:112063; Jones et al. 2020)

facts.text: Near Huron and Kettleman City, the ground sank more than 7 inches between July 2013 and March 2015.
When groundwater is pumped out, the soil compacts and the surface sinks, sometimes for good. That can crack canals and cut how much water they carry.
NISAR images in L-band (about 24 cm wavelength), which keeps a better lock on the ground in vegetated farmland.
NISAR looks to the left and repeats every track every 12 days. Track 042 missed two passes over this frame: 5 Feb and 4 Aug 2026.
